Prior authorization means a provider asks before treatment for assurance that Medicare will pay. In WISeR, a participating company uses AI and other technology to review whether documentation meets Medicare rules; CMS says a licensed clinician determines any recommendation not to pay.

The useful distinction is between a payment checkpoint and a treatment decision: a payment review can delay care, but it is not the same as an AI choosing a treatment. Providers can instead proceed to review after service and before payment.

The pilot covers selected services in Original Medicare—the federal fee-for-service program, distinct from private Medicare Advantage plans—in Arizona, New Jersey, Ohio, Oklahoma, Texas and Washington. CMS says it excludes emergencies, inpatient-only services and services whose delay would pose substantial risk.

CMS pays vendors a share of spending it considers averted, adjusted by quality scores. The payment guide reduces the multiplier to 95 or 90 percent for lower scores and requires quarterly audits. The records do not show how well those safeguards corrected poor decisions.

On September 8, the Electronic Frontier Foundation published internal Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services records about WISeR, Medicare’s AI-assisted prior-authorization pilot. The records show rollout problems, but they do not support EFF’s claim that two vendors denied more than 20,000 requests.

The cited March 30 table reports 20,397 total decisions for two vendors: 14,453 affirmations and 5,944 non-affirmations. An affirmation is an advance decision that the submitted request meets Medicare's requirements. A non-affirmation means the request was not approved at that decision point; it may later be corrected, resubmitted or appealed. The table does not report 20,000 final denials of care.

Other records still document trouble. Before the January launch, Innovaccer told CMS its system would not be fully functional and planned to auto-affirm—approve automatically—requests for 45 to 60 days while it finished testing. A March 30 report listed 123 Genzeon requests at least three days old, including one 83 days old. It divided them among vendor-response, decision-letter and correction stages, without identifying the oldest case’s stage.

sources.authority: Current primary program description for WISeR scope, review mechanism, safeguards, participants and payment design.
passages: The WISeR Model helps protect American taxpayers by leveraging enhanced technologies, such as Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML), along with human clinical review, to ensure timely and appropriate Medicare payment for select items and services.
WISeR will run for six performance years from January 1, 2026 to December 31, 2031 in six states: New Jersey, Ohio, Oklahoma, Texas, Arizona, and Washington.
WISeR does not change Medicare coverage or payment policy.
The model excludes inpatient-only services, emergency services, and services that would pose a substantial risk to patients if delayed.
All recommendations for non-payment are determined by appropriately licensed clinicians who will apply standardized, transparent and evidence-based procedures to their review.
WISeR does not apply to people with Medicare Advantage and will have no impact on them.

Providers and suppliers for people with Original Medicare in selected regions will have the choice of submitting a prior authorization request for the model’s selected items and services or going through a post-service/pre-payment review.

Model participants receive a percentage of the expenditures associated with averted wasteful, inappropriate care as a result of their reviews. That percentage is adjusted based on the participant’s performance on measures related to the process, including provider experience.
sources.limitation: This is CMS's current description of its own model and safeguards. It does not answer each problem in the released records or independently establish how well every vendor followed the requirements.

source.passage: The WISeR Model helps protect American taxpayers by leveraging enhanced technologies, such as Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML), along with human clinical review, to ensure timely and appropriate Medicare payment for select items and services. WISeR will run for six performance years from January 1, 2026 to December 31, 2031 in six states: New Jersey, Ohio, Oklahoma, Texas, Arizona, and Washington. WISeR does not change Medicare coverage or payment policy. The model excludes inpatient-only services, emergency services, and services that would pose a substantial risk to patients if delayed. All recommendations for non-payment are determined by appropriately licensed clinicians who will apply standardized, transparent and evidence-based procedures to their review. WISeR does not apply to people with Medicare Advantage and will have no impact on them. Providers and suppliers for people with Original Medicare in selected regions will have the choice of submitting a prior authorization request for the model’s selected items and services or going through a post-service/pre-payment review. Model participants receive a percentage of the expenditures associated with averted wasteful, inappropriate care as a result of their reviews. That percentage is adjusted based on the participant’s performance on measures related to the process, including provider experience.

sources.authority: Primary documents for the payment design, audit safeguard, pre-launch vendor warning and dated operational tables cited in the article.
passages: Page 322, Table 2 lists 20,397 year-to-date decisions received for Virtix and Zyter through the March 30, 2026 report: 6,096 for Virtix and 14,301 for Zyter.

Page 322, Table 3 splits those 20,397 decisions into 14,453 affirmations and 5,944 non-affirmations. Virtix has 2,863 affirmations and 3,233 non-affirmations; Zyter has 11,590 affirmations and 2,711 non-affirmations.

Page 22 says payment savings are calculated from non-affirmations not followed by an affirmed resubmission or a successfully appealed claim denial. It also says one series of non-affirmations for the same beneficiary, item or service, and provider within 120 days earns only one participant payment.

Page 234 says that as of March 30 Genzeon had 123 prior-authorization requests aged three days or older, with the oldest 83 days. It separates them into 14 awaiting a model-participant response, 44 awaiting a decision letter and 65 awaiting correction for creation of a tracking number or dismissal. The page does not say which stage applied to the oldest request.

In a December 12, 2025 letter on pages 216 and 217, Innovaccer said it would meet the January 5, 2026 go-live date without full functionality. It cited changing requirements, new integration expectations, unclear governance and insufficient end-to-end testing time, and planned to auto-affirm requests while completing a phased rollout.

Page 217 says Innovaccer expected the initial auto-affirmation period to last approximately 45 to 60 days and described the approach as a way to avoid a backlog of unprocessed requests while it finished, validated and deployed the full rules-based solution.

Page 99 sets quality multipliers at 100 percent for aggregate scores of 85 to 100 percent, 95 percent for scores of 60 to 84 percent and 90 percent below 60 percent. It also says CMS conducts quarterly audits of participant records for consistency with Original Medicare coverage criteria.

Page 410 groups January requests for two vendors into one-to-five, six-to-ten and eleven-to-twenty-one-day buckets. Those buckets do not disclose an exact rate for responses inside or outside 72 hours.
sources.limitation: The review was bounded to seven cited pages plus direct checks of the complete file's identity and page count, not a claim to have substantively reviewed every one of 443 pages. Operational tables are dated snapshots and some are cumulative; they must not be added together. Non-affirmation is not synonymous with a final denial of care.

sources.authority: Independent June 23 reporting for patient/provider experience, CMS and vendor responses, and program background before the September records release.
passages: KFF reported on June 23 that patients, doctors and other health professionals it interviewed described confusion, errors, long waits and stress during WISeR's rollout.

KFF reported that an Oklahoma Medicare beneficiary made an extra two-and-a-half-hour drive after learning his regular procedure needed preapproval and declined a proposed third trip that he understood was for paperwork.
Humata CEO Jeremy Friese told KFF that its system gives an ‘immediate yes’ in 88 percent of cases for which clinical data supports an approval.
Zyter CEO Sundar Subramanian told KFF that the company continuously monitors operations and works with stakeholders to address questions and improve provider experience.
CMS official Abe Sutton told KFF that the model aims to reduce inappropriate care without delaying appropriate care and that payment backlogs were being resolved.
KFF reported clinicians' suspicion of AI-generated errors, while Humata's CEO said he had not heard about AI hallucinations.
sources.limitation: This is June background, not new September reporting. The reported experiences establish real concerns and attributed accounts, not that AI caused every delay, that every non-affirmation was wrong or that the same conditions continued unchanged through September.
